title: Neonatal immune development in neonates born small and large for gestational age
summary:
Medicine is constantly developing. Many improvements in medical care are only possible through research involving people. This is especially important for newborn and premature babies, as their immune systems work differently from those of adults. However, we still know relatively little about how their immune systems develop.
Babies born prematurely or with a low birth weight have a higher risk of developing infections. We do not yet fully understand why this is the case. Learning more about how their immune systems work could help us find better ways to prevent and treat infections in the future.
In this study, we want to learn more about how the immune system develops during the first two years of life. We will study premature and full-term babies who are born with either a lower or higher birth weight and compare their immune systems with those of babies born at a normal birth weight. We hope this will help us understand why babies with a low birth weight are more likely to develop infections.
We will also include newborn babies with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) in our study and follow their development over time. Children with trisomy 21 have certain differences in how their immune systems work and are more likely to develop severe infections. We hope that our study will help us better understand how their immune systems develop during the first two years of life.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Small, appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA), or large term newborns (SGA, AGA, or LGA), or
2. Small, appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA), or large preterm newborns (SGA, AGA, or LGA), or
3. Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), and
4. Age less than 168 hours (7 days) at the time of inclusion.
5. Written informed consent provided by the legal guardians.
6. Gestational age at birth ≥ 24+0/7 weeks of gestation.
7. Optionally, the mothers of the preterm and term newborns included in the study may also participate.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Severe medical conditions (e.g. major congenital abnormalities). This exclusion criterion does not apply to children with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).
2. Severe congenital conditions (e.g. hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy) in full-term newborns.
3. For mothers who may optionally participate in the study only: no intention to breastfeed.
